newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. envoy urges fast action on Nazi gold search.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy urges fast action on Nazi gold search.

text.p: The United States ambassador to Switzerland on Wednesday urged fast action to establish whether pre-World War Two deposits by victims of the Nazi Holocaust against the Jews were still held in Swiss banks.

But the envoy, Madeleine May Kunin, indicated Washington accepted that the Swiss authorities -- who last month pledged to begin a wide-ranging study on the question -- were keen to settle an issue that could harm ties between the two countries.

"I think the sooner, the better that we shed light and present the facts in the question....The time has come to set the record straight," declared the Swiss-born ambassador, a former Deputy Secretary of Education.
"The Swiss have made clear they want a credible, transparent process, and we agree," she told the American International Club of Geneva.
Kunin, who served three terms as governor of Vermont state, took up her appointment in Berne, the Swiss capital, in August, just as the so-called "Nazi gold" affair was breaking.

Apart from lost deposits by Holocaust victims, it has broadened into a controversy over whether gold looted in occupied countries and sold to Swiss banks to fund the Nazi military machine might still be held in Switzerland.

The Swiss government issued a decree at the end of September setting up a commission of experts empowered to bypass tight bank secrecy rules to produce an historical account of Swiss commerce with Nazi Germany.

It will also review how much wealth was deposited with Swiss banks and other financial organisations by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution and whether enough has been done to identify lost assets of those who died in the Holocaust.
Legislation already adopted by the lower house of parliament in Berne and expected to pass the upper house in December gave the commission five years to complete its work.
But the U.S. ambassador, who left Switzerland with her family in 1940 to settle in the United States, said she felt it was important that the work be completed within a much tighter time-frame.
"The sooner all the information is made public, the better it will be for everybody," she declared.

A demand by New York Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, for a U.S. investigation into what he has called "50 years of deception" by Switzerland has caused bitter resentment in the country.

Newspaper commentators in both German- and French-speaking Switzerland, while agreeing that the whole issue must be thoroughly aired, have suggested the problem has been raised to undermine the Swiss position as a major world banking centre.

The affair has coincided with publication through the World Jewish Congress (WJC) of wartime U.S. intelligence reports alleging the Swiss-run International Committee of the Red Cross was infiltrated by the Nazis.

In response to demands from D'Amato and the WJC, the U.S. State Department said last week it would scour its own archives for information on what happened to gold and other assets looted by the Nazis.
Swiss banks and international Jewish groups set up a separate panel last May to search for any Holocaust accounts and return the assets to the legal heirs of the depositors.
